For newly hatched Dichelopandalus bonnieri larvae, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0007 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0007 grams], a value estimated from the typical egg diameter of 1.1 millimeters observed in congeneric pandalids. Size at the onset of planktonic life is quite modest, reflecting the relatively small yolk reserves available during embryonic development. Field surveys conducted in the North Atlantic suggest that the time since birth at birth is roughly 152.5 days [ab = roughly 152.5 days] when water temperatures remain at a consistent 10 °C [T = 10 °C], which is typical for the deeper portions of this species' depth range. This prolonged embryonic incubation, spanning approximately five months, ensures that newly hatched zoea larvae emerge during periods of elevated spring productivity, thereby maximizing the availability of suitable phytoplankton prey for first exogenous feeding. The brood eggs themselves are carried by ovigerous females, which maintain a steady brooding posture to ensure adequate oxygenation of the developing embryos throughout this extended incubation window.

Larval development proceeds through a series of free-swimming zoea stages before the metamorphic climax is reached. In Dichelopandalus bonnieri, the time since birth at metamorphosis has been recorded at 122 days  under a stable thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This milestone marks the transition from a planktonic larva to a post-larval juvenile, involving a substantial reorganisation of the body plan. At this point, the carapace length at metamorphosis is typically 0.5 centimeters , indicating a juvenile of sufficient size to commence benthic foraging. The allometric shift that accompanies this moulting event allows the growing juvenile to exploit different food resources and microhabitats, reducing competition with conspecific larvae that may still occupy the water column. This stage is particularly vulnerable to predation, as the recently metamorphosed juvenile lacks the full defensive capabilities of the adult form.

The period spent as a post-metamorphic juvenile is characterised by steady somatic growth and progressive development of the reproductive system. For females of Dichelopandalus bonnieri, the time since metamorphosis at puberty is 480 days [tp = 480 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. At this point, the carapace length at puberty for females reaches 1.4 centimeters [Lp = 1.4 centimeters], a size that signifies the onset of gonad maturation and the ability to produce a clutch of fertilised ova. This synchronised developmental schedule ensures that females are entering the reproductive population after accumulating sufficient energy reserves to support egg production and brooding. The transition from an immature post-metamorphic crustacean to a sexually mature adult involves significant hormonal changes that regulate the timing of the pubertal moult, after which the female becomes ovigerous during the breeding season.

Male development follows a slightly more accelerated trajectory compared to females in this protandric species. For males, the carapace length at puberty is 1.1 centimeters [Lp = 1.1 centimeters], reached after a time since metamorphosis at puberty of 300 days [tp = 300 days] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This smaller size at sexual maturation reflects the different reproductive strategies employed by males, who allocate resources toward the production of spermatophores rather than eggs. Following their first pubertal moult, males function as reproductively viable organisms, participating in mating events during the spawning season. Over subsequent moults and growing seasons, some individuals may undergo sex change, transitioning from functional males to females as they increase in size. This phenomenon is common among pandalid shrimps and allows the population to maintain a balance between male and female reproductive capacity across different size classes.

In terms of maximum longevity, Dichelopandalus bonnieri individuals have a lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days] when maintained at a controlled temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], which equates to approximately five years of potential life. The ultimate carapace length attained by the largest individuals is 2.0 centimeters [Li = 2.0 centimeters], representing the asymptotic size reached after several years of gradual moult increments. Natural mortality in this species is often associated with senescence following the final reproductive season, during which the physiological condition of the animal declines and its ability to withstand environmental stressors weakens. Comparisons with other pandalids suggest that this lifespan is intermediate, falling between the shorter-lived temperate species and the longer-lived deep-water forms. The combination of a modest adult size and a multi-year life history allows this whip shrimp to sustain stable populations across its boreal distribution, despite periodic fluctuations in food availability and predation pressure from demersal fish stocks.
